title: Accelerating inverse materials design using generative diffusion models with reinforcement learning - Nature Machine Intelligence
text:
Download PDF

AbstractDiffusion models promise to accelerate materials design by directly generating novel structures with desired properties, but existing approaches such as conditional generation typically require expensive and substantial labelled data (>10,000) and lack adaptability. Here we present MatInvent, a general and efficient reinforcement learning workflow that optimizes diffusion models for goal-directed crystal generation. By formulating equivariant denoising as a multistep decision-making problem, MatInvent leverages policy gradient with reward-weighted Kullback–Leibler regularization, including experience replay and diversity filters to enhance optimization efficiency and sample diversity. For single-objective designs, MatInvent rapidly converges to target values within 60 iterations (~1,000 property evaluations) across electronic, magnetic, mechanical, thermal and physicochemical properties. Furthermore, MatInvent achieves robust optimization in design tasks with multiple conflicting properties, successfully proposing low-supply-chain-risk magnets and high-κ dielectrics. Compared with state-of-the-art methods, MatInvent exhibits comparable or superior generation performance under specified property constraints while markedly reducing the demand for property computation. Compatible with diverse diffusion model architectures and property constraints, MatInvent could offer broad applicability in materials discovery.

Machine Learning Applications in Materials Design

MainThe development of novel functional materials is pivotal for accelerating scientific progress in various fields such as catalysis, microelectronics and renewable energy1,2,3. The key objective is to identify property-optimal candidates within an enormous design space. Existing methods include iterative experimental trial and error4,5 and high-throughput screening6,7. However, the brute-force screening of all possible materials is prohibitive, a challenge circumvented through expert-defined search spaces. Although this approach has offered success in discovering novel materials, manually constraining the search space could introduce negative bias.Recently, generative models8,9,10,11,12, particularly diffusion models13,14,15,16,17, have emerged as promising frameworks for generating novel and theoretically stable inorganic crystal structures spanning the entire periodic table. Several methods, such as conditional generation by classifier-free guidance14, have been proposed to steer diffusion models towards generating materials with targeted properties18,19,20. Nevertheless, these methods require substantial pre-existing labelled data for model fine-tuning, limiting their generalizability and flexibility across diverse inverse design tasks.Reinforcement learning (RL) provides a framework for optimizing generative models by iterative exploration of complex problem spaces on the basis of feedback rewards, with potential to improve generation quality and controllability21,22,23. This approach decouples learning from dense annotations by leveraging sparse or indirect reward signals, requiring substantially fewer labelled data compared with supervised fine-tuning22,23. Notably, RL has become a mainstream strategy for optimizing Simplified Molecular Input Line Entry System (SMILES)-based language models to accomplish goal-directed molecular generation24,25,26,27,28. The previous RL approaches for crystals focus on structure prediction of a given composition29,30 or composition generation within a narrow chemical space31, neither of which addresses de novo generation of complete three-dimensional (3D) crystal structures with target properties. Concurrent works32,33,34,35 also explore RL for crystal generation, yet lack a general framework compatible with diverse diffusion model architectures and materials properties. Furthermore, few studies have investigated key techniques for improving optimization efficiency and sample diversity in RL fine-tuning of crystal generative models.This work proposes MatInvent, a versatile and efficient RL workflow for optimizing pretrained diffusion models towards objective-driven crystal generation. By framing denoising generation as a multistep decision-making problem, MatInvent leverages policy optimization with reward-weighted Kullback–Leibler (KL) regularization, including experience replay and diversity filters to enhance sample efficiency and diversity. For single-objective optimization, MatInvent demonstrates remarkable performance and flexibility across various materials design tasks encompassing electronic, magnetic, mechanical, physicochemical, thermal and synthesizability properties. Compared with the conditional generation of MatterGen, our RL approach substantially reduces the requirement for labelled data while exhibiting enhanced generative performance under target property constraints. Furthermore, MatInvent achieves robust optimization in design tasks with multiple competing objectives, successfully designing magnets with low supply-chain risk and high-κ (dielectric constant) gate dielectrics. This versatility makes our approach highly appealing to researchers in materials science, chemistry and catalysis.ResultsRL pipelineMatInvent is an RL workflow designed for goal-directed generation of crystalline materials (Fig. 1). In the pipeline, the diffusion model acts as the RL agent that generates novel 3D crystal structures through a T-step reverse denoising process on atomic types, atomic coordinates and lattice matrices13,14. The denoising process of the diffusion model can be reframed as a T-step Markov decision process (MDP)22,23 for our online RL algorithms (Methods). We denote the diffusion model before RL fine-tuning, which was pretrained on large-scale unlabelled datasets of crystal structures (for example, Alex-MP14) and can generate diverse crystalline materials spanning over 80 elements, as the prior. In each RL iteration, the diffusion model randomly generates a batch of m crystal structures. The generated structures undergo geometry optimization using universal machine learning interatomic potentials (MLIPs)36 and their energy above hull (Ehull) is calculated. Only crystal structures that are thermodynamically stable (Ehull < 0.1 eV per atom), unique and novel (SUN)14 are retained after filtering, in which n samples are randomly selected for property evaluation and assigned corresponding rewards. The materials properties and rewards can be obtained through theoretical simulations, ML predictions and empirical calculations. The top k samples ranked by reward are used to fine-tune the diffusion model on the basis of policy optimization with reward-weighted KL regularization (Methods). The KL regularizer between the pretrained and fine-tuned models is incorporated into the RL objective function to prevent reward overfitting while preserving the materials knowledge acquired during pretraining22. Moreover, experience replay and the diversity filter are respectively employed to improve optimization efficiency and sample diversity of the RL process, enabling faster convergence towards the target while generating novel and diverse crystal structures. Experience replay is used to improve the stability and efficiency of learning by storing past high-reward crystals in a replay buffer and reusing them during RL fine-tuning27,37. The diversity filter imposes a linear penalty on the reward of non-unique crystal structures on the basis of the number of previous occurrences38,39. Specifically, crystals with the same structure or composition as previously generated samples are assigned reduced rewards and subsequently removed from the replay buffer, thereby encouraging the diffusion model to explore unseen materials space. Notably, MatInvent is a general-purpose RL workflow that is compatible with different diffusion model architectures (Supplementary Section C.1). Unless otherwise specified, all experiments in this work use the MatterGen14 framework as the diffusion model in the RL process.Fig. 1: MatInvent workflow for goal-directed materials generation.Full size imagea, A schematic overview of MatInvent methodology. In each RL iteration, the diffusion model acts as the RL agent to generate a batch of 3D crystal structures, which are subsequently geometrically optimized using machine learning potentials. Only valid SUN structures are retained after filtering, proceeding to target property evaluation and reward assignment. High-reward samples are then used to fine-tune the diffusion model by policy optimization with reward-weighted KL regularization, aided by experience replay and a diversity filter to enhance sample efficiency and diversity. b, The impact of geometry optimization (opt) and SUN filtering before property evaluation on the SUN ratio of generated structures during the RL process targeting a density of 18.0 g cm−3. c, The effect of experience replay on the optimization efficiency of the RL process targeting a density of 18.0 g cm−3. d, The role of the diversity filter in the composition diversity of generated structures during the RL process with a target density of 18.0 g cm−3.Source dataTo investigate the importance of individual components in our RL workflow, ablation studies were conducted using the materials design task with a target density of 18.0 g cm−3 (Supplementary Section C.2). Two metrics, the SUN ratio and composition diversity ratio, are defined to evaluate the generation quality and diversity of materials structures from diffusion models (Supplementary Section B). As shown in Fig. 1b and Supplementary Section C.2.1, MLIP-based geometry optimization and SUN filtering before property evaluation improve both the SUN ratio and composition diversity of the generated structures during the RL process. As depicted in Fig. 1c and Supplementary Section C.2.2, experience replay enhances the RL optimization efficiency, enabling faster convergence to the target property value with fewer property evaluations. This is particularly important for materials properties that have expensive evaluation costs. Moreover, the diversity filter can encourage diffusion models to explore different chemical systems and achieve a higher diversity ratio of chemical compositions during the RL process (Fig. 1d and Supplementary Section C.2.3). This facilitates the design of diverse crystal structures with target properties and prevents the RL optimization from stagnating in local minima.Single-property optimizationIn numerous applications, such as energy storage, superconductivity and electronic devices, the primary demand lies in designing novel materials with targeted or enhanced properties. MatInvent was evaluated on different inverse design tasks for single-property optimization. These tasks encompass various properties of inorganic materials, including electronic, magnetic, mechanical, thermal, physicochemical and synthesizability characteristics. The property values and corresponding rewards are derived from density functional theory (DFT) calculations (Fig. 2a,b), MLIP simulations (Fig. 2c,d) or ML prediction models (Fig. 2e–g). The first task (Fig. 2a) aims to generate materials with a target band gap of 3.0 eV, a key property for light-emitting devices40, photocatalysis41 and wide-band-gap semiconductors42. In the second task (Fig. 2b), the goal is to design materials with magnetic densities higher than 0.2 Å−3, a prerequisite for permanent magnets14. The third task (Fig. 2c) involves generating novel inorganic compounds with specific heat capacities exceeding 1.5 J g−1 K−1, which is crucial for thermal energy storage and high-temperature protection materials43. The fourth task (Fig. 2d) focuses on designing novel crystal structures with strong epitaxial matching to the commercially dominant Si(100) substrate, requiring a minimal co-incident area (MCIA) below 80 Å2 (ref. 44). A lower MCIA indicates a higher degree of matching between the thin-film material and the substrate, which is crucial for materials synthesis techniques such as chemical vapour deposition and sputtering44. The fifth task (Fig. 2e) targets the generation of materials with a high bulk modulus of 300 GPa, an essential property for superhard and aerospace materials45. The sixth task (Fig. 2f) focuses on discovering new materials with high total dielectric constants exceeding 80, important for applications such as electronic devices and supercapacitors46,47. The seventh task (Fig. 2g) investigates the generation of materials with high synthesizability scores on the basis of feedback from the ML model48, aiming to design novel and experimentally synthesizable materials. Finally, the eighth task (Fig. 2h) is to design new materials with low supply-chain risk, requiring a Herfindahl–Hirschman index (HHI) score49 below 1,250 directly computed through PyMatGen50. Further details of the RL experiments and reward calculation are provided in Supplementary Sections E.1 and E.2, while the methods for materials property evaluation are described in Supplementary Section D.Fig. 2: MatInvent performance on single-property optimization.Full size imagea–h, The optimization curves (left) for RL and visualizations of some generated crystal structures (right) on different design tasks with a single target property (grey dashed lines represent target values): band gap equal to 3.0 eV (a); magnetic density higher than 0.2 Å−3 (b); specific heat capacity exceeding 1.5 J g−1 K−1 (c); MCIA below 80 Å2 on the Si(100) substrate (d); bulk modulus of 300 GPa (e); total dielectric constants exceeding 80 (f); synthesizability score higher than 0.9 (g); HHI score below 1,250 (h). Curves show mean values across independent RL runs (n = 6 for c–h; n = 3 for a,b), each contributing its per-loop mean property value; shading (error band) indicates s.d. across runs.Source dataAs shown in Fig. 2, across all tasks, the average property values of the generated materials progressively approach the target values with successive RL iterations. Remarkably, within 60 iterations and ~1,000 property evaluation calls, the average property values converge to their targets for most tasks. Six more single-objective design tasks were also explored (Supplementary Section E.3), involving shear modulus, Young’s modulus, Pugh ratio, formation energy, crustal abundance and price. Moreover, the property distributions of the SUN structures generated by the RL fine-tuned model displayed a clear shift, and became more concentrated around the target values compared with the pretrained model (Supplementary Section E.4). This confirms that MatInvent can optimize diffusion models and steer their generative distribution towards regions of materials with desired properties. As depicted in Supplementary Section E.5, most RL fine-tuned models exhibited higher SUN ratios (>45%) than did the initial pretrained model (38.7%), which can be attributed to MLIP-based structure optimization and SUN filtering before property evaluation. All results demonstrate that MatInvent is an efficient and general RL framework for diffusion models in single-property inverse design tasks.We further compared MatInvent with the state-of-the-art conditional generation method (MatterGen14), on two specific tasks: targeting materials with band gaps of 3.0 eV and magnetic densities exceeding 0.2 Å−3. For a fair comparison, all RL experiments used the same unconditional MatterGen model pretrained on the Alex-MP-20 dataset as the initial model14; more details are in Supplementary Section E.6. For MatterGen’s conditional generation, the pretrained model with adaptor modules undergoes fine-tuning on pre-existing and DFT-labelled datasets, subsequently applying classifier-free guidance to steer crystal generation towards the desired objectives14. As illustrated in Fig. 3a, MatInvent needs only 1,600 DFT calculations to obtain rewards for 100 RL iterations, substantially reducing the high DFT costs required for model fine-tuning compared with MatterGen’s conditional generation (Supplementary Section E.9). Moreover, the RL-fine-tuned model demonstrates approximately twice the SUN ratio compared with the conditional generation of MatterGen (Fig. 3b). Further details are listed in Supplementary Section E.5 regarding individual values of stability, uniqueness and novelty for unconditional MatterGen, conditional generation and MatInvent.Fig. 3: Comparison between conditional generation and RL.Full size imagea, Number of DFT-labelled data used for model fine-tuning in the MatInvent workflow and conditional generation of MatterGen across two inverse design tasks. b, SUN ratios of generated structures from MatterGen conditional generation and RL-fine-tuned diffusion model following the MatInvent workflow. SUN ratios were calculated using MatterGen’s method and code14, with stability assessed using the MatterSim MLIP36 (more details in Supplementary Section B.1). c,d, Probability density distributions of property values of SUN structures generated by RL-fine-tuned diffusion models and MatterGen’s conditional generation for inverse design targets of magnetic density higher than 0.2 Å−3 (c) and band gap of 3.0 eV (d). e,f, Number of SUN structures satisfying property requirements discovered by MatterGen conditional generation and RL-fine-tuned diffusion models within 250 DFT property calculations, for targets of magnetic density higher than 0.2 Å−3 (e) and band gap of 3.0 ± 0.1 eV (f).Source dataIn Fig. 3c, the two methods achieve comparable performances on the magnetic density task, with property distributions of SUN structures similarly concentrated around the target value. In contrast, in Fig. 3d, the RL-fine-tuned model substantially outperforms MatterGen’s conditional generation on the band-gap task, yielding a distribution much more sharply peaked at the target of 3.0 eV. We also evaluated the performance of MatInvent against MatterGen’s conditional generation in discovering SUN structures that satisfy stringent property requirements under limited DFT calculation budgets. As shown in Fig. 3e, the RL-fine-tuned model identified 27 SUN structures with magnetic densities exceeding 0.2 Å−3 within a budget of 250 DFT property calculations, performing similarly to MatterGen conditional generation (23 structures). Figure 3f reveals that the RL-fine-tuned model discovered 43 SUN structures with band gaps of 3.0s ± 0.1 eV after 250 DFT property calculations, substantially surpassing the conditional generation of MatterGen (11 structures). It is worth noting that tasks with narrow property-range constraints present challenges comparable to those with extreme target properties. All results demonstrate that MatInvent achieves comparable or improved goal-directed crystal generation performance while reducing DFT computational burden. This arises because RL directly optimizes the diffusion model to maximize rewards, concentrating generation in high-reward regions, whereas conditional generation requires learning the complete conditional probability distribution over the target property.Multiple-property optimizationMost materials design problems require finding structures that satisfy multiple property constraints. Two tasks were designed to evaluate the performance of MatInvent in the simultaneous optimization of multiple materials properties. The first task focuses on designing novel permanent magnets with low supply-chain risk, aiming to avoid the utilization of rare-earth elements14. This task can be formulated as satisfying two property constraints: (1) magnetic density higher than 0.2 Å−3 and (2) HHI score below 1,500. An HHI score below 1,500 is considered indicative of low supply-chain risk49. In the RL experiments, the DFT method was employed to determine the magnetic densities of the generated structures, and PyMatGen50 was utilized to compute their HHI scores. The minimum between the scaled values of magnetic density and HHI score served as the reward for each sample during the online RL process, thereby facilitating the simultaneous optimization of both target properties, and avoiding overoptimizing the easier objective while neglecting the harder one (Supplementary Section F.2). As illustrated in Fig. 4b, the average values of both properties for the generated SUN structures gradually approached the target region with successive RL iterations, ultimately converging near the desired values after 100 iterations. In contrast to the initial phase of RL (loops 0–20), the distribution of both properties for SUN structures generated during loops 100–120 exhibited a pronounced shift and became narrowly concentrated around the target values, as demonstrated in Fig. 4a. These findings demonstrate that MatInvent can iteratively optimize the diffusion model and its generation distribution for two competing materials properties.Fig. 4: Designing permanent magnets with low supply-chain risk.Full size imagea, Property distribution of SUN structures generated during the initial (0–20 loops) and final (100–120 loops) stages of the RL process. b, Mean values of target properties of SUN structures generated in each RL iteration. The grey dashed lines represent the target values. c, Number of DFT-labelled data used for model fine-tuning (left) and SUN ratios of generated structures (right) for MatterGen conditional generation and MatInvent workflow. SUN ratios were calculated using MatterGen’s method and code14, with stability assessed by the MatterSim MLIP36 (more details in Supplementary Section B.1). d, Number of SUN structures satisfying property requirements found by MatterGen conditional generation and RL-fine-tuned diffusion models within 200 DFT property calculations, for targets with magnetic density above 0.2 Å−3 and HHI score below 1,500. e, Visualizations of some SUN structures generated by RL-fine-tuned diffusion models, along with their chemical formula, space group, Ehull, magnetic density, HHI score and synthesizability score.Source dataAs depicted in Fig. 4c, MatInvent requires only 1,920 DFT property calculations for 120 RL iterations, and achieves much higher SUN ratio than that of MatterGen’s conditional generation (about three times)14. Moreover, we compared the performance between the RL-fine-tuned diffusion model and MatterGen’s conditional generation in discovering SUN structures that meet two property requirements under limited DFT computation budgets (Supplementary Section F.3). As shown in Fig. 4d, the RL-fine-tuned diffusion model identified 14 SUN structures satisfying both property requirements under 200 DFT property calculations, outperforming MatterGen’s conditional generation (11 SUN structures). Of the 14 SUN structures found by MatInvent, 78.6% (n = 11) exhibit ML-predicted synthesizability scores above 0.5, indicating potential experimental feasibility48. Some of these structures are presented in Fig. 4e. Overall, all results establish that MatInvent is highly efficient for inverse design tasks with multiple objectives, achieving superior crystal generation performance while markedly reducing DFT computational costs.The second task aims to design novel high-κ dielectrics, critical components in numerous microelectronic devices, including CPUs, dynamic random-access memory and high-frequency antennas46,47. Their performance depends on an intricate balance between a high dielectric constant and a wide band gap, two inversely correlated characteristics that rarely coexist within a single material46,47. Moreover, a high figure of merit (FoM) is desirable to suppress tunnelling current; one top experimentally reported high-κ dielectric, t-HfO2, exhibits an FoM of approximately 210 (ref. 47). Consequently, the second task can be formulated with three optimization objectives: band gap (Eg) exceeding 3.0 eV, total dielectric constant (εtotal) surpassing 30 and FoM higher than 210 (ref. 47). Given the computational expense of DFT property evaluation, ML models were employed to predict Eg, εtotal and the corresponding FoM (=Egεtotal) of the crystal structures generated during the RL process (Supplementary Section F.2). Incorporating the FoM objective into the RL reward is intended to guide the diffusion model in generating crystal structures that achieve a balanced improvement in both band gap and total dielectric constant, rather than overoptimizing a single property (Supplementary Section F.4).As illustrated in Fig. 5a, the structures generated during early-stage RL (0–20 iterations) fall into two primary categories: high Eg but low εtotal, and low Eg but high εtotal. After 220 RL iterations, the property distributions of generated SUN structures exhibited a pronounced shift towards the target region, with high Eg and εtotal, compared with the initial phase of RL (0–20 iterations). Correspondingly, the Pareto front was progressively optimized during the RL iterations (Fig. 5b), continuously advancing towards the region of high Eg and high εtotal. These results demonstrate that MatInvent can achieve Pareto optimization for two conflicting materials properties. Subsequently, 2,048 crystal structures were generated by the RL-fine-tuned diffusion model and ranked according to ML-predicted FoM values, from which 200 structures were selected for DFT validation. As depicted in Fig. 5c, over 95% of the structures exhibit a DFT-calculated Eg exceeding 3.0 eV, which benefits from RL fine-tuning and the accurate predictive model for Eg. In contrast, only about 20% of the structures possess a DFT-calculated εtotal higher than 30, potentially resulting from the poor εtotal prediction accuracy of the ML model (Supplementary Section D.3.5). Despite the inevitable errors in ML predictions, the DFT property distribution after RL fine-tuning shows a substantial shift compared with the pretrained model (Fig. 5e). Most structures exhibit DFT-calculated FoM exceeding 120, with four structures achieving FoM values greater than 400. Within a budget of 200 DFT property evaluations, MatInvent successfully identified 17 SUN structures that satisfy all three target criteria (Fig. 5d), highlighting its superior performance in Pareto optimization. The grey dashed lines represent the target values. d, Number of SUN structures satisfying property requirements found by RL-fine-tuned diffusion models within 200 DFT property calculations, for objectives of Eg exceeding 3.0 eV, εtotal surpassing 30 and FoM higher than 210. e, Distribution of DFT-computed FoM for structures generated by the pretrained and RL-fine-tuned diffusion models. f, Visualizations of some SUN structures generated by RL-fine-tuned diffusion models, along with their chemical formula, space group, Ehull, synthesizability score, Eg, εtotal and FoM.Source dataDiscussionMatInvent is a versatile and efficient RL workflow that can tailor the generation of pretrained diffusion models towards novel materials structures with desired properties. This workflow implements policy optimization with reward-weighted KL regularization, experience replay and diversity filters to ensure efficient optimization and diverse sampling. Across various single-objective design tasks spanning from electronic, magnetic, mechanical, thermal and physicochemical properties to synthesizability, MatInvent demonstrates excellent optimization performance, with fast convergence to target values within approximately 60 iterations (1,000 property evaluations). Moreover, MatInvent exhibits robust optimization capabilities in design tasks involving multiple conflicting objectives, even with low-precision rewards. Compared with conditional generation approaches that require substantial labelled data for target properties, MatInvent achieves comparable or enhanced generative performance in both single- and multiobjective inverse design while reducing the demand for property assessment. We also discuss the practical applicability of MatInvent in Supplementary Section E.7. MatInvent is applicable to two distinct scenarios: (1) when labelled data are absent or scarce and (2) when a reasonably sized labelled dataset is available, whereas conditional generation is typically limited to scenario 2.For materials design tasks where property evaluation must rely on expensive calculations, this evaluation step becomes the primary computational bottleneck governing the overall speed of RL fine-tuning. To mitigate this, we adopt a hybrid graphics processing unit (GPU)–CPU computing strategy: sample generation and model fine-tuning are performed on GPU nodes, while DFT calculations for RL rewards are dispatched in parallel to a CPU cluster. A per-job time limit of 2 h is enforced to prevent non-converging calculations from stalling entire iterations, and timed-out jobs receive no reward and are discarded. Further acceleration may be achieved through ML-accelerated DFT surrogates or uncertainty-aware predictors that selectively invoke full DFT calculations only for high-uncertainty or high-value candidates.Despite these strengths, there are several promising directions to enhance MatInvent. The current RL workflow relies on external property evaluators such as ML prediction models and DFT calculations, which may introduce noise and potential biases into the reward signal. Future extensions could incorporate uncertainty-aware or differentiable property predictors to provide informative gradients and enhance learning robustness51. Moreover, real-world materials design tasks frequently involve more than five objectives with varying degrees of importance. Techniques such as curriculum learning52,53, Pareto set learning54 and preference-conditioned policies55 are worth exploring to enhance MatInvent’s performance in multiobjective optimization. Furthermore, materials synthesis information, such as precursor availability, synthetic route constraints and synthesizability criteria, which is important for experimental validation and autonomous laboratories, could be integrated into the RL framework.MatInvent offers a general and efficient route to inverse materials design. Its versatility enables extension to diverse materials classes by employing different diffusion models, including perovskites, metal–organic frameworks56,57 and two-dimensional materials58. The framework can be further adapted to various practical applications, such as catalysis, superconductivity59 and quantum computing19, using carefully designed RL rewards and property evaluation methods. Moreover, the integration of MatInvent into automated laboratories could offer a compelling avenue for achieving closed-loop materials discovery. This general and efficient workflow is poised to attract widespread attention in the materials research community.MethodsRepresentation of crystal structuresThe periodic structure of crystals arises from the repeating arrangement of atoms in 3D space, and the simplest repeating unit is defined as the unit cell. A unit cell with N atoms can be described by \({\mathscr{ \mathcal M }}=(A,X,L)\), where \(A=[{{\bf{a}}}_{1},{{\bf{a}}}_{2},\ldots ,{{\bf{a}}}_{N}]\in {{{{\mathbb{R}}}}}^{h\times N}\) represents the one-hot encoding of atom types, \(X=[{{\bf{x}}}_{1},{{\bf{x}}}_{2},\ldots ,{{\bf{x}}}_{N}]\in {{{{\mathbb{R}}}}}^{3\times N}\) symbolizes atoms’ Cartesian coordinates and \(L=[{{\bf{l}}}_{1},{{\bf{l}}}_{2},{{\bf{l}}}_{3}]\in {{{{\mathbb{R}}}}}^{3\times 3}\) expresses the crystal lattice matrix. The volume of a unit cell V = |det(L)| must be non-zero, meaning that L is invertible. On the basis of periodic boundary conditions, the atomic positions within the unit cell can also be described using fractional coordinates F = L−1X = [f1, f2, …, fN] ∈ [0, 1)3×N, which are widely used in crystallography and crystal generation. Thus, a unit cell with N atoms can also be described by \({\mathscr{ \mathcal M }}=(A,F,L)\), and the infinite crystal structure can be represented as$$\{({{\bf{a}}}_{i}^{^{\prime} },{{\bf{f}}}_{i}^{^{\prime} })| {{\bf{a}}}_{i}^{{\prime} }={{\bf{a}}}_{i},{{\bf{f}}}_{i}^{{\prime} }={{\bf{f}}}_{i}+L{\bf{k}}{{\bf{1}}}_{N},{\rm\forall }{\bf{k}}\in {{{{\mathbb{Z}}}}}^{3}\}$$

The general algorithmic formulation of such models is detailed in Supplementary Section A.1. Implementation details for specific model architectures, including MatterGen14, can be found in their original references.The diffusion models involve two Markov chains: a forward noising process on atom types, atomic fractional coordinates and lattice matrix, and a reverse denoising process learned by a graph neural network. For the data distribution q0 of 3D crystal structures, \({{{\mathcal{M}}}}_{0} \sim {q}_{0}\left({{{\mathcal{M}}}}_{0}\right)\). The diffusion model approximates q0 with a parameterized (θ) graph neural network by denoising process in the form \({p}_{\theta }({{\mathscr{ \mathcal M }}}_{0})=\int {p}_{\theta }({{\mathscr{ \mathcal M }}}_{0:T})\,{\rm{d}}{{\mathscr{ \mathcal M }}}_{1:T}\), where \({p}_{\theta }\left({{{\mathcal{M}}}}_{0:T}\right)\) is calculated using$${p}_{\theta }\left({{{\mathcal{M}}}}_{0:T}\right)={p}_{T}\left({{{\mathcal{M}}}}_{T}\right){\prod }_{t=1}^{T}{p}_{\theta }\left({{{\mathcal{M}}}}_{t-1}| {{{\mathcal{M}}}}_{t}\right),$$
(2)
and in the timestep t can be described by$${p}_{\theta }({{\mathscr{ \mathcal M }}}_{t-1}| {{\mathscr{ \mathcal M }}}_{t})={\mathscr{ \mathcal N }}({\mu }_{\theta }({{\mathscr{ \mathcal M }}}_{t},t),{\sigma }_{t}^{2}I),$$
(3)
where \({\mu }_{\theta }\left({{{\mathcal{M}}}}_{t},t\right)\) is predicted by the graph neural network.On the basis of the approximate posterior \(q({{{\mathcal{M}}}}_{1:T}| {{{\mathcal{M}}}}_{0})\), the denoising process is the reverse of a forward noising process. In the forward process, Gaussian noises are gradually added to \({{\mathcal{M}}}\) according to a variance schedule β1, …, βT:$$\begin{array}{c}q({{\mathscr{ \mathcal M }}}_{1:T}| {{\mathscr{ \mathcal M }}}_{0})={\prod }_{t=1}^{T}q({{\mathscr{ \mathcal M }}}_{t}| {{\mathscr{ \mathcal M }}}_{t-1}),\\ q({{\mathscr{ \mathcal M }}}_{t}| {{\mathscr{ \mathcal M }}}_{t-1})={\mathscr{ \mathcal N }}(\sqrt{1-{\beta }_{t}}{{\mathscr{ \mathcal M }}}_{t-1},{\beta }_{t}I).\end{array}$$

Training the diffusion model is conducted by maximizing a variational lower bound on the log likelihood \({{\mathbb{E}}}_{q}\left[\log {p}_{\theta }\left({{{\mathcal{M}}}}_{0}\right)\right]\), which is equivalent to optimizing the following objective:$${\mathscr{ \mathcal L }}(\theta )={{\mathbb{E}}}_{t \sim {\mathscr{ \mathcal U }}\{0,T\},{{\mathscr{ \mathcal M }}}_{t} \sim q({{\mathscr{ \mathcal M }}}_{t}| {{\mathscr{ \mathcal M }}}_{0})}[{\parallel \widetilde{{\boldsymbol{\mu }}}({{\mathscr{ \mathcal M }}}_{0},t)-{{\boldsymbol{\mu }}}_{\theta }({{\mathscr{ \mathcal M }}}_{t},t)\parallel }^{2}]$$

where \(\widetilde{{\boldsymbol{\mu }}}\) is the posterior mean of the forward process.RL for crystal diffusion modelsAn MDP formalizes sequential decision-making problems. It can be characterized by a tuple (S, A, ρ0, P, R), where S denotes the state space, A represents the action space, ρ0 is the initial state distribution, P specifies the transition kernel and R defines the reward function. In every step t, the agent observes a state st ∈ S, selects an action at ∈ A, obtains a reward R(st, at) and transforms into a subsequent state st+1 ~ P(st+1∣st, at). The agent’s behaviour is determined by its policy π(a∣s). As the agent interacts with the MDP, it generates trajectories of states and actions τ = (s0, a0, s1, a1, …, sT, aT). The goal of RL is to optimize π to maximize the expected cumulative reward JRL(π) over sampled trajectories:$${ \mathcal J }_{\mathrm{RL}}(\pi )={{\mathbb{E}}}_{\tau \sim p(\tau |\pi )}[{\sum }_{t=0}^{T}R({s}_{t},{a}_{t})].$$
(6)
Our online RL algorithms formulate the denoising process of the diffusion model as an MDP and optimize diffusion models for crystal generation with target properties22,23. Given a crystal diffusion model \({p}_{\theta }({{{\mathcal{M}}}}_{0:T})\) parameterized by θ and the final reward \(r({{{\mathcal{M}}}}_{0})\) of crystal \({{{\mathcal{M}}}}_{0}\) involving single or multiple target materials properties, the denoising process can be reframed as a T-step MDP:$$\begin{array}{c}{s}_{t}={{{\mathcal{M}}}}_{T-t},\quad {a}_{t}={{{\mathcal{M}}}}_{T-t-1},\\ {\rho }_{0}\left({s}_{0}\right)=({{\mathcal{N}}}(0,{{\boldsymbol{I}}}),{{\mathcal{U}}}(0,1)),\quad P\left({s}_{t+1}| {s}_{t},{a}_{t}\right)={\delta }_{{a}_{t}},\\ \pi \left({a}_{t}| {s}_{t}\right)={p}_{\theta }\left({{{\mathcal{M}}}}_{T-t-1}| {{{\mathcal{M}}}}_{T-t}\right),\\ R\left({s}_{t},{a}_{t}\right)=\left\{\begin{array}{ll}r\left({s}_{t+1}\right)=r\left({{{\mathcal{M}}}}_{0}\right)\quad &\,{\mbox{if}}\,t=T-1,\\ 0\quad &\,{\mbox{otherwise}}\,\end{array}\right.\end{array}$$
(7)
where δy is the Dirac delta distribution with non-zero density only at y. Sampling the initial state s0 of a trajectory is similar to sampling the first state \({{\mathscr{ \mathcal M }}}_{T}=({A}_{T},{F}_{T},{L}_{T})\) of the denoising generation, in which AT and LT are sampled from \({{\mathcal{N}}}(0,{{\boldsymbol{I}}})\) and FT is sampled from \({{\mathcal{U}}}(0,1)\). The cumulative reward of every trajectory is equal to \(r\left({{{\mathcal{M}}}}_{0}\right)\), because all intermediate rewards are 0, as only the final state \({{{\mathcal{M}}}}_{0}\) of the denoising process is meaningful for computing crystal properties and rewards. Therefore, optimizing π is equivalent to fine-tuning the diffusion model. The common goal in RL fine-tuning of diffusion models is to maximize the expected reward of the generated crystals:$${{{\mathcal{J}}}}_{{{\rm{RL}}}}(\theta )={{\mathbb{E}}}_{{p}_{\theta }({{{\mathcal{M}}}}_{0})}\left[r\left({{{\mathcal{M}}}}_{0}\right)\right].$$
(8)
As depicted in Supplementary Section A.2, the gradient of this objective is$${\nabla }_{\theta }{{{\mathcal{J}}}}_{{{\rm{RL}}}}={{\mathbb{E}}}_{{p}_{\theta }\left({{{\mathcal{M}}}}_{0:T}\right)}\left[r\left({{{\mathcal{M}}}}_{0}\right){\sum }_{t=1}^{T}{\nabla }_{\theta }\,\log \,{p}_{\theta }\left({{{\mathcal{M}}}}_{t-1}| {{{\mathcal{M}}}}_{t}\right)\right].$$
(9)
The risk of fine-tuning solely on the basis of rewards related to target properties is that the diffusion model may overfit to the rewards and move too far away from the initial state (pretrained model)22. To retain the broad materials knowledge that the diffusion model has learned from the pretraining dataset for generating reasonable and valid crystal structures, we add the reward-weighted KL between the pretrained and current fine-tuned models as a regularizer to the objective function according to$${{\mathbb{E}}}_{{p}_{\theta }\left({{{\mathcal{M}}}}_{0:T}\right)}\left[(\lambda -r\left({{{\mathcal{M}}}}_{0}\right)){\sum }_{t=1}^{T}{\mathrm{KL}}\,\left({p}_{\theta }\left({{{\mathcal{M}}}}_{t-1}| {{{\mathcal{M}}}}_{t}\right)\parallel {p}_{{{\rm{pre}}}}\left({{{\mathcal{M}}}}_{t-1}| {{{\mathcal{M}}}}_{t}\right)\right)\right],$$
(10)
where λ is a constant slightly larger than the maximum reward; more details are in Supplementary Section A.3. The reward weight allows the current diffusion model to appropriately move away from the pretrained model24, thereby encouraging the model to shift its distribution to higher-reward regions. Thus, the final gradient to optimize the RL objective is$$\begin{array}{l}-\alpha r\left({{{\mathcal{M}}}}_{0}\right){\sum }_{t=1}^{T}{\nabla }_{\theta }\,\log \,{p}_{\theta }\left({{{\mathcal{M}}}}_{t-1}| {{{\mathcal{M}}}}_{t}\right)\\ +\beta (\lambda -r\left({{{\mathcal{M}}}}_{0}\right)){\sum }_{t=1}^{T}{\nabla }_{\theta }\,{\mathrm{KL}}\left({p}_{\theta }\left({{{\mathcal{M}}}}_{t-1}| {{{\mathcal{M}}}}_{t}\right)\parallel {p}_{{{\rm{pre}}}}\left({{{\mathcal{M}}}}_{t-1}| {{{\mathcal{M}}}}_{t}\right)\right)\end{array}$$
(11)
where α and β are the weights of reward and KL regularization, respectively.Experience replayThe experience replay27,37 is integrated into MatInvent, and is used to improve the stability and efficiency of RL by storing past high-reward crystals and reusing them during model fine-tuning. It breaks the correlation between consecutive experiences by sampling from a buffer of previous experiences (called the replay buffer) rather than relying only on the most recent experience. Specifically, the size of the replay buffer is set to 100. When the number of stored crystal structures exceeds this capacity, only the 100 structures with the highest rewards are retained. In each RL iteration, 10 crystal structures are randomly sampled from the replay buffer and combined with the top 50% rewarded structures from the current iteration for model fine-tuning. After fine-tuning, the top 50% rewarded structures are added to the replay buffer, applying a deduplication criterion whereby only the highest-rewarded structure is preserved for each unique chemical composition.Diversity filter (DF)We draw inspiration for DFs from refs. 38,39 with small modifications. Here, DFs linearly penalize crystals with non-unique chemical compositions on the basis of the number of previous occurrences, which acts as a more lenient version of the unique DF, that is, to directly truncate the reward to 0 (ref. 38). The reward is transformed according to the number of previous occurrences (Occ) beyond an allowed tolerance (Tol) until a hard threshold is reached, referred to as the buffer (Buff):$$\,{\mbox{Filtered}}\;{\mbox{reward}}\,=\left\{\begin{array}{ll}r\left({{{\mathcal{M}}}}_{0}\right)\times \dfrac{{{\rm{Occ}}}-\,{\mbox{Tol}}}{{\mbox{Buff}}-{\mbox{Tol}}\,}&\,{\mbox{if}}\,{{\rm{Tol}}} < {{\rm{Occ}}} < \,{\mbox{Buff}}\,\\ r\left({{{\mathcal{M}}}}_{0}\right)&\,{\mbox{if}}\,\quad \,{\mbox{Occ}}\le {\mbox{Tol}}\,\\ 0&\,{\mbox{if}}\,\quad \,{\mbox{Occ}}\ge {\mbox{Buff}}\,\end{array}\right.$$
(12)
where Tol is set to 3 and Buff is set to 6. A selective memory purge will be triggered for materials structures that remain in the replay buffer but are penalized by the diversity filter, resulting in their removal from the replay buffer27. That is, crystals with the same chemical composition as previously generated samples are assigned reduced rewards and subsequently removed from the replay buffer.Reporting summaryFurther information on research design is available in the Nature Portfolio Reporting Summary linked to this article.

Data availability

The diffusion models were pretrained on the open-source Alex-MP14 or MP-20 (refs. 9,60) datasets, which are available via GitHub at https://github.com/microsoft/mattergen. Checkpoint files for the diffusion model and property prediction model are available via Hugging Face at https://huggingface.co/jwchen25/MatInvent and archived on Zenodo at https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.22770457 (ref. 61). Source data are provided with this paper.
Code availability

The source code for MatInvent is available via GitHub at https://github.com/schwallergroup/matinvent and archived on Zenodo at https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.22769927 (ref. 62).
